911.title: Craft the job
911.hook: researchers found hospital cleaners who shaped their jobs around patients' care found more meaning (Wrzesniewski and Dutton, 2001)
911.howItsDone: People who practice job crafting look for small changes within their role: adjusting a task, building a relationship, or reframing the work around the people it serves; some also hold their daily tasks as an offering, in the spirit of Herbert's poem.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the week with one thing: every switch has a toll, and Ecclesiastes says do it with thy might. Your line was practicing the way back. Did you get your stretch without switching? Today, the same job, done two different ways. Day nine hundred eleven.

Two people clean the same hospital ward. Same mop, same pay, same list. One of them describes the job as cleaning rooms. The other talks about the patients: which one likes the blinds open, which one hasn't had a visitor, how to time the floors so nobody is woken. When researchers Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton looked at people like these, the second kind of cleaner saw the work as part of healing, and found more meaning in it. Nobody had rewritten their job description. They had reshaped the job themselves. Today: job crafting.
screen: `SAME MOP, SAME LIST.` → `THE BLINDS, THE VISITOR, THE FLOORS.` → `THEY CHANGED IT THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Wrzesniewski and Dutton called this job crafting: the ways people quietly reshape the work they've been given. Their paper describes three. First, the tasks. You can add, drop or change what you do, or how you do it. The cleaner who times the floors so a patient can sleep has changed a task, without asking anyone. Second, the relationships. You can change who you deal with and how. Some cleaners talked with patients and families, and saw themselves as part of the care team. The list never mentioned conversation. They added it. Third, the way you see it. You can change what you think the job is for. Cleaning rooms, or helping people heal: the work is identical, and the meaning isn't. Now a neighbor from much further back. The poet and priest George Herbert wrote a short poem called The Elixir, about doing ordinary things for God. One stanza says: "Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, Makes that and th' action fine." For Herbert, the sweeping stays sweeping. What changes is what it's done for, and that changes both the room and the act. The researchers don't speak of God, and Herbert didn't run a study. They are describing something that rhymes: the same task can be lifted by how it's held. Fourth, a caution. Job crafting isn't a way to excuse bad pay or bad bosses; some jobs need changing from the outside, too. But inside a lot of work there's a little room to move, and that room is yours.
screen: `CHANGE THE TASKS.` · `CHANGE THE RELATIONSHIPS.` · `CHANGE HOW YOU SEE IT.` · `WHO SWEEPS A ROOM.` · then, large: `CRAFT THE JOB.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, hold your own work in mind, paid or unpaid, a job, a home, a study, a care you give. Breathe slowly. First, picture one task you do often. Is there a small way to do it differently? Second, picture one person your work touches. Could you meet them a little more fully? Third, ask what the work is for, underneath the list. Don't decide anything yet. Just let one possibility rise, and hold it. The bell holds the time.
Job crafting. The ways people quietly reshape the tasks, relationships and meaning of the work they've been given. Today's word.
Your line: that room is yours. Today, reshape one small part of your work: one task done differently, one person met more fully, or one moment remembering what it's for. Day nine hundred eleven.

fork.reveal: cleaners who crafted their jobs timed their work around patients' rest. the list didn't say to; they saw their work as part of the care.

what it means: people quietly reshape their work, its tasks, its relationships and its meaning, from the inside.

912.title: Unpaid, not unvalued
912.hook: caring, housework and volunteering are work, and traditions honor them
912.carry: I saw what you did, and it mattered
912.howItsDone: Sikhs perform seva at gurdwaras by cooking and serving langar, cleaning and caring for visitors; in some Jewish homes the poem from Proverbs 31 is sung at the Friday night table.

segments.voice: Yesterday, job crafting: the hospital cleaners who reshaped their own jobs, and Herbert's line about sweeping a room. Your line was that room is yours. What did you reshape? Today, the work nobody pays for at all. Day nine hundred twelve.

Who washed the dishes after dinner last night? Who sat up with the feverish child, drove the grandparent to the appointment, folded the laundry, coached the team, made the casserole for the neighbor after the funeral? None of it shows up on a paycheck. When someone asks, so what do you do, almost none of it gets mentioned. And yet a household, a street, a congregation would start to fall apart without it. Today: unpaid.
screen: `DISHES, FEVERS, RIDES, CASSEROLES.` → `NOT ON ANY PAYCHECK.` → `WITHOUT IT, THINGS FALL APART.`

segments.voice: First, a name for it. Unpaid work is still work. Caring for children or the sick, keeping a home running, volunteering: they take time, skill and energy, just like paid jobs. The only thing missing is the money, and money is not the only measure of worth. Second, a very old portrait. The last chapter of the book of Proverbs, in the Hebrew Bible, praises a capable woman. Much of what it honors is the work of a household: she rises while it's still night, provides food, makes cloth, opens her hand to the poor. One verse says, "She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness." In some Jewish homes, this poem is sung at the Friday night table. Housework, in that text, is not invisible. It's sung about. Third, a word from Sikh tradition: seva, selfless service. At a gurdwara, the Sikh place of worship, volunteers cook and serve langar, a free communal meal open to anyone who walks in. Others wash the dishes, sweep the floors, or care for visitors' shoes. Nobody is paid. In Sikh teaching, this is not a lesser task than worship; seva is itself a way of serving God and the community, and anyone may take part, whatever their standing. Fourth, what this asks of us. If unpaid work is real work, then the people doing it deserve real thanks. Not a vague nod at holidays, but a specific word: I saw what you did, and it mattered. That kind of noticing costs nothing, and it can be given tonight.
screen: `UNPAID WORK IS STILL WORK.` · `THE BREAD OF IDLENESS.` · `SEVA, SELFLESS SERVICE.` · `I SAW WHAT YOU DID.` · then, large: `UNPAID, NOT UNVALUED.`

segments.voice: Let the unpaid work around you come into view, for these two minutes. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind a meal someone cooked for you, a bed someone made, a ride someone gave, a hard day someone sat through with you. Let one person stand out. See their hands doing the work. Then let your own unpaid work come to mind, too, the things you do that nobody counts. Hold both without a ledger. If you pray, you can hold that person in your tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Unpaid. Work done without wages, caring, housework, volunteering, that is still real work, and honored in the old texts and traditions. Today's word.
Your line: I saw what you did, and it mattered. Today, thank one person for a specific piece of unpaid work they do. Name the work, not just the person. Day nine hundred twelve.

what it means: caring, housework and volunteering are real work, and traditions honor them.
what a scholar hears: Proverbs 31 sung at the Friday table, and Sikh seva, where cooking and dishwashing are themselves a way of serving God.

913.title: Not my worth
913.carry: what was lost was held, not who you are
913.howItsDone: People facing job loss often lean on community, faith or philosophy to keep their sense of worth apart from their work; Stoic readers return to Epictetus's sorting of what is and isn't in our power, and Jewish and Christian readers turn to the book of Job.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dishes and the fevers and the langar: work nobody pays for. Your line was I saw what you did, and it mattered. Whom did you thank? Today, what's left of a person when the work is gone. Day nine hundred thirteen.
screen: `I SAW WHAT YOU DID, AND IT MATTERED.`

segments.voice: The badge stops working at the door. Or the email arrives with a meeting invitation from someone in human resources. Or the shop that was going to last forever puts a sign in the window. Or the body says no more to the job it did for years. However it comes, losing work can feel like losing a name. At a party, someone asks, so what do you do? And for a while there's no easy answer. Today: Epictetus.
screen: `THE BADGE STOPS WORKING.` → `SO WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `NO EASY ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, the confusion. A job gives us a schedule, colleagues, a title, a paycheck, and a ready answer at parties. It's easy to fuse all of that into a sense of who we are. Then, when the job goes, it can seem as if we've gone with it. Second, a Stoic teacher. Epictetus taught philosophy in the Roman world. His handbook opens with a sorting of the world: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Among the things he says are not in our power: our body, our property, our reputation, our offices, the positions we hold. What is in our power is how we judge, what we aim for, what we turn away from. For Epictetus, a person's worth lives on that inside list. A job is on the outside list. It can be given and taken. In his view, it was never the measure of a person. Third, a man who lost everything. In the book of Job, in the Hebrew Bible, Job loses his wealth, his household, his children, all in one day. And he says, "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Later in the book he argues, mourns and protests at length, and the text lets him. Some readers hear a distinction in that first line: what was given can be taken, and the one it was given to is still there. Fourth, what this is not. It isn't a claim that losing work doesn't hurt, or doesn't matter. Rent matters. Purpose matters. Grief is fair, and Job is given room for it. Epictetus, for his part, would ask for a cooler sorting. What the two share is a narrower line: what was lost was held, not who you are, and the person who held it is still there.
screen: `A JOB FUSED WITH A SELF.` · `IN OUR POWER, AND NOT.` · `THE LORD GAVE, AND HATH TAKEN.` · `IT HURTS, AND IT'S NOT YOUR WORTH.` · then, large: `NOT MY WORTH.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, sort the way Epictetus did. Breathe slowly. Picture two baskets. In the outer basket, place the things that can be given and taken: a title, a desk, a salary, how others see you. Set them in gently, one at a time. Now notice what's left in you, as you sit here breathing: the way you pay attention, what you care about, how you choose to meet this day. That's the inner basket. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Epictetus. The Stoic teacher who sorted the world into what's in our power and what isn't, and put a job on the outside list. Today's word.

Your line: what was lost was held, not who you are. Today, when someone asks what you do, or when you ask yourself, add one thing about who you are that has nothing to do with a job. Day nine hundred thirteen.

fork.reveal: he lists offices, the positions we hold, with body, property and reputation: not in our power. what is in our power is how we judge and what we aim for.

trapdoor: what you thought: losing a job means losing part of yourself.
what it means: work can be given and taken, and losing it hurts, but your worth isn't what went.
what a scholar hears: Epictetus's opening sorting in the Enchiridion, with offices on the not-in-our-power side, and Job's line that what was given can be taken from one who remains.

914.title: The stopping days
914.hook: Friday prayers, Shabbat, Sunday, Buddhist observance days: many traditions stop work on purpose
914.howItsDone: Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall; Muslims gather for the Friday congregational prayer at midday; Christians commonly gather on Sunday, and some keep it as a day of rest; Buddhist lay followers may keep extra precepts on uposatha days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epictetus's two lists, and a job on the outside one. Your line was what was lost was held, not who you are. What did you name about yourself that has nothing to do with work? Today, the days when work stops on purpose. Day nine hundred fourteen.
screen: `WHAT WAS LOST WAS HELD, NOT WHO YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: A Friday at midday, and a shopkeeper pulls down the shutter and walks toward the mosque. A Friday at sunset, and a family lights candles and the phones go into a drawer. A Sunday morning, and church bells over quiet streets. A full-moon day, and a woman in white walks to a Buddhist temple to keep extra precepts until the next morning. Different calendars, different reasons. But each of these is a stopping, chosen on purpose and kept together. Today: the stopping days.
screen: `A SHUTTER, CANDLES, BELLS, WHITE.` → `DIFFERENT CALENDARS.` → `STOPPING ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Each tradition stops in its own way, so let's take them one at a time. First, Shabbat. The Ten Commandments in Exodus say, "Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work." Then the verse keeps going: not you, nor your son or daughter, nor your servants, nor your animals, nor the stranger within your gates. The rest is for everyone in the household, including those who work for you. Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. Second, Friday in Islam. The Qur'an tells believers, when the call to the Friday congregational prayer is heard, to hurry to the remembrance of God and leave their trading; and when the prayer is done, to go out and seek God's bounty again. So Friday is not a full day off in the way Shabbat is. It's a stopping in the middle of the day, for prayer together. Third, Sunday. The book of Revelation speaks of being "in the Spirit on the Lord's day," and Christian tradition came to read the Lord's day as Sunday, the day of the resurrection. Some Christians keep it as a day of rest; others gather and then go about the day; and some, such as Seventh-day Adventists, keep the seventh day, Saturday. Fourth, Buddhist observance days, called uposatha. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha teaches lay followers to keep extra precepts on these days, for a night and a day following the example of the awakened ones. These days don't ask for the same thing. What they share is a refusal to let work fill every hour.
screen: `SHABBAT: REST FOR EVERYONE.` · `FRIDAY: LEAVE YOUR TRADING.` · `SUNDAY: THE LORD'S DAY.` · `UPOSATHA: EXTRA PRECEPTS.` · then, large: `THE STOPPING DAYS.`

segments.voice: Practice the stop. Let your hands fall still. If something in you is still working, planning, answering, let it hear the shutter come down. Breathe. Then, gently, look ahead at your week. Is there an afternoon, an evening, a morning, that could become a stopping time, kept on purpose? Don't schedule it yet. Just find it, and imagine the quiet in it. The bell holds the time.
The stopping days. Shabbat, the Friday prayer, the Lord's day, the uposatha: times traditions set apart from work on purpose, each in its own way. Today's word.
Your line: the stopping days. Today, plan a stopping time for this week: a day, or part of one, with work put away. Tell someone, so it's kept together. Day nine hundred fourteen.

915.title: Wealth used well
915.hook: the Buddha praises wealth earned rightly and shared (Anguttara Nikaya 4.61); Paul warns of loving money (1 Timothy 6:10)
915.howItsDone: Buddhist householders read the Buddha's teaching on right use of wealth as a guide to providing for family and giving; some Christians turn to 1 Timothy 6 when thinking about money, generosity and contentment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shutter coming down at midday, candles at sunset, bells on Sunday, white clothes on an observance day. Your line was the stopping days. Did you find a stopping time this week? Today, what work leaves in our hands: money. Day nine hundred fifteen.

"Money is the root of all evil." The line gets passed around as if it were scripture. It isn't, quite. The real verse says something sharper, and it's worth getting right. And from a very different tradition, there's a teaching that sounds almost the opposite at first: the Buddha speaking warmly to a householder about earning and enjoying wealth. Put the two side by side, and they turn out to be asking a similar question. Not whether you have money. What it's doing. Today: Anathapindika.
screen: `THE ROOT OF ALL EVIL?` → `NOT QUITE.` → `WHAT IS IT DOING?`

segments.voice: First, the verse as it actually reads. In the first letter to Timothy, which tradition ascribes to Paul: "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows." The love of money. Not money itself. The problem is where the heart is fastened, and the picture is vivid: people piercing themselves through. Second, the same letter, a few lines later. Those who are rich are told not to trust in uncertain riches, and to be "rich in good works, ready to distribute." The letter doesn't tell the rich to stop being rich. It tells them what wealth is for. Third, the Buddha to a householder. In a discourse in the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha speaks with Anathapindika, a wealthy lay follower. He praises wealth gained by effort and the sweat of the brow, gained rightly, without harm. And he describes what to do with it: make yourself happy, and your parents, your family, the people who work for you, and your friends; guard against misfortune like fire and flood; make offerings to relatives, guests and those who have died; and give to those living a holy life. Wealth spent like that, he says, has been put to good use. Fourth, the shared question. The letter to Timothy warns about loving money; the Buddha praises using it well. Neither treats money as holy or as filth. Each points past the money to the person holding it: how it was earned, and where it goes. Two traditions, each in its own words, asking what your money is doing today.
screen: `THE LOVE OF MONEY.` · `RICH IN GOOD WORKS.` · `EARNED RIGHTLY, USED WELL.` · `WHAT IS IT DOING?` · then, large: `WEALTH USED WELL.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, follow the money you have in a calm, unhurried way. Breathe slowly. First, picture where it came from: the work, the hours, the effort it stands for. Let yourself honor that. Then picture where it went this week: food, rent, a gift, a coffee, something forgotten. Don't judge any of it. Just notice. Then let one sum come to mind, small or large, that you could spend in a way the Buddha's list would recognize: making someone glad, or guarding against hard times, or giving. Hold it there. The bell holds the time.
Anathapindika. The wealthy follower the Buddha taught to earn rightly and spend it on family, guests and those living a holy life. Today's word.
Your line: put to good use. Today, spend one sum, however small, on purpose: to make someone glad, to prepare for a hard day, or to give. Day nine hundred fifteen.

916.title: A tenth
916.hook: Christian tithes, Muslim zakat, Sikh dasvandh: each tradition sets aside a share
916.howItsDone: Some Christians tithe a tenth of their income to their church; Muslims calculate and pay zakat each year on qualifying wealth; Sikhs who keep dasvandh set aside a tenth of their earnings, often through the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the love of money, and the Buddha's householder told to put his wealth to good use. Your line was put to good use. What did you spend on purpose? Today, the share some traditions set aside before anything else. Day nine hundred sixteen.

A paycheck lands. Before the rent, before the groceries, before anything else, a small piece is moved somewhere else: an envelope in a church, a transfer to a mosque's fund for the poor, a donation box at a gurdwara. For some who give this way, this isn't charity left over at the end of the month, if there's anything left. It's set aside on purpose, sometimes before anything else is paid. Today: a tenth.
screen: `A PAYCHECK LANDS.` → `OFF THE TOP.` → `THE FIRST THING PAID.`

segments.voice: First, the tithe. In Genesis, after a battle, Abram meets Melchizedek, a priest and king, and "he gave him tithes of all." The letter to the Hebrews, looking back on that scene, spells it out: Abraham "gave the tenth of the spoils." Later, the prophet Malachi says, "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house." Some Christians today give a tenth of their income to their church; others see the tenth as a guide rather than a rule, and give in their own measure. Second, zakat. The Qur'an pairs prayer with zakat, a required giving, and it names who should receive it, among them the poor, the needy, those in debt and the traveler. Zakat isn't a tenth of income; Muslim teaching sets it as a share of certain kinds of wealth, and the share differs from one kind to another. But like the tithe, it's not optional generosity. It's an act of worship, and in Muslim teaching it purifies the wealth that remains. Third, dasvandh. In Sikh tradition, dasvandh is the practice of setting aside a tenth of one's earnings for the community and those in need, often given through the gurdwara, where it can help keep the free kitchen running. Fourth, what they share. The amounts and rules differ, and each tradition has its own reasons. But each one sets a share aside on purpose and regularly. That turns giving from a mood into a habit. And each, in its own way, treats part of what comes in as belonging to others.
screen: `THE TITHE: A TENTH OF ALL.` · `ZAKAT: PRAYER'S PARTNER.` · `DASVANDH: A TENTH FOR OTHERS.` · `A SHARE SET ASIDE ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `A TENTH.`

segments.voice: Imagine the share, for these two minutes. Picture the money that comes to you this month, from a paycheck, an allowance, a pension, whatever it is. Now picture setting aside a small piece first, before anything else, and putting it in an envelope marked for others. It doesn't need to be a tenth. Notice what happens in you as you set it aside. Then picture where it might go: a person, a cause, a community. The bell holds the time.
A tenth. The tithe, the Sikh dasvandh, and alongside them the Muslim zakat: a share of what comes in, set aside on purpose for others. Today's word.
Your line: a share for others. Today, set aside a small share of what you have, any amount, and decide where it will go. Day nine hundred sixteen.

917.title: Ambition, examined
917.howItsDone: Christians read Mark 10:43–44 as a teaching that greatness means serving others, and Hindus who study the Bhagavad Gita read 2.47 as guidance on working fully without clinging to the results.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tenth: the tithe, zakat and dasvandh, each tradition setting aside a portion. Your line was a share for others. Did a small share leave your hands? Today, the end of the week, and a harder word. Day nine hundred seventeen.

Two brothers walk up to their teacher on the road and ask for a favor before they'll say what it is. In Mark's Gospel they are James and John, fishermen who once left their nets to follow Jesus. The request, when it comes, is blunt: when you come into your glory, let one of us sit at your right hand, and the other at your left. The other ten disciples hear about it, and Mark says they are much displeased with the brothers. Mark doesn't say why. Some readers suspect the ten wanted the same seats. Today's word is the wish that walked up to Jesus on the road: ambition.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS ASK A FAVOR.` → `THE RIGHT HAND AND THE LEFT.` → `THE TEN ARE DISPLEASED.`

segments.voice: Start with what Jesus doesn't do. He doesn't tell them to stop wanting to be great. He calls them to him and turns the ladder upside down. In the King James Bible: "whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: and whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all." The wish stays. Its direction changes. Ambition isn't erased; it's handed a job. Second, a voice that climbed all the way up. The book of Ecclesiastes speaks as a king in Jerusalem who built houses, planted vineyards, and gathered silver and gold. Then he turns and looks at all of it: "all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun." He reached what he aimed at, and it couldn't tell him what it was for. Third, a teaching from India. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that his right is to the work itself, never to its fruits; he shouldn't let the fruits be his motive, and he shouldn't cling to doing nothing either. Some readers hear in this a way to strive with everything while loosening the grip on the prize. Fourth, the question all three leave on the table. Ambition can serve, or it can consume, and the difference may lie less in how much someone wants than in what the wanting is for. A promotion that lets someone protect a team is one thing; the same promotion as a scoreboard is another. This week the work days asked how to shape a job, what unpaid work is worth, what we're worth without work, when to stop, how to use money, and what to share. Ambition asks the question under all of them.
screen: `THE GREAT ONE SERVES.` · `NO PROFIT UNDER THE SUN.` · `THE WORK, NOT THE FRUITS.` · `SERVE OR CONSUME?` · then, large: `WHAT IS IT FOR?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring one ambition to mind, large or small: a job, a number, a finished project, a name on a door. Hold it plainly, without judging it. Now ask it one question: what are you for? Let the first answer come. Then ask the same question of that answer. Keep going, gently, until the answers stop changing. It might end at safety, or love, or someone you want to provide for, or simply wanting to be seen. Any of these can be honest. If you pray, you can hold that last answer in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Ambition. The wish to rise. In Mark's Gospel Jesus doesn't forbid it; he points it toward serving. Today's word.
Your line: what is it for. Today, before you chase the next goal, the next reply, the next number, ask it that question once, and listen to the answer. Day nine hundred seventeen.

fork.setup: you're one of the other ten disciples, and you've just heard James and John asked for the best seats. what does Mark say the ten did?
options: laughed it off.
were much displeased with James and John.

fork.reveal: the ten were much displeased. then Jesus calls them all together and turns greatness into service.

original.note: Sanskrit, Bhagavad Gita 2.47: your right is to the work alone.

trapdoor: what you thought: ambition is either a virtue or a vice.
what it means: a wish to rise that can serve or consume, depending on what it's for.
what a scholar hears: Mark 10:43–44, where Jesus doesn't forbid the wish to be great but redefines it: the great one shall be your minister.
